synopsis: The booklet defines hypothesis testing as assessing an observed difference against a null hypothesis of no real difference; validation sample sizes must match the claim, with binomial detection tests sized by significance, power and the separation between acceptable and unacceptable probabilities [f14228, f5448, f5453]. For old-versus-new warning systems, it recommends paired recording on the same machine and hazards: McNemar's test uses only discordant outcomes, illustrated by 12 hazards caught only by the new system versus 3 caught only by the old, while separate deployments confound site, operator and weather [f14237, f14233, f14234, f14235, f14236]. Sequential tests can stop early on clearly good or bad evidence, but acceptance thresholds and statistical tests must be fixed in advance [f6903, f644]. Checking hundreds of scenario cells individually at 95% confidence risks chance-driven passes or failures, so primary claims should be predefined and multiplicity or simultaneous-confidence methods used where claims must hold together [f7485, f7486]. As an on-road scale illustration, RAND's April 2016 analysis estimated about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% fatality-rate improvement with 95% confidence and 80% power; that estimate concerns autonomous road vehicles, not a supplied off-road validation sample size [f6663, f6923, f14263].
